q: UserService validates sign-up data, saves the user to the database and builds the welcome email text. Marketing rewords the email, and the change forces a retest of the saving code. Which principle is broken?
options: Single Responsibility: it has several unrelated reasons to change
Open/Closed: a class must never be edited again once it has shipped
Liskov Substitution: UserService cannot replace its base class
Interface Segregation: the class has too many public methods
why: Validation rules, storage and email wording change for different reasons and are owned by different people. In one class, a wording change touches and risks the saving code. Splitting them gives each reason to change its own class.
wrong: OCP is about adding behaviour without rewriting stable code, not a ban on edits, and the pain here comes from mixed jobs.
No inheritance is involved, so there is nothing to substitute.
Method count is not the issue; ISP is about clients depending on methods they do not use.

q: To follow SRP, a teammate splits a Money class (add, subtract and compareTo on an amount and currency) into MoneyAdder, MoneySubtractor and MoneyComparer, one method each. What is the problem?
options: Nothing: SRP means one public method per class, so the split is correct
The three new classes should extend one base class so they still count as one
The methods change for the same reason; splitting them scatters one concept
SRP only applies to classes that talk to a database or a file
why: SRP is about reasons to change, not method count. Every Money operation depends on the same rules for amount and currency, so they change together. Splitting them lowers cohesion: one rule change now touches three classes that must stay in sync.
wrong: This is the most common SRP myth; a class can have many methods that serve one purpose.
A shared base class does not undo the split; the money logic is still spread across three places.
SRP applies to any code; I/O is just a frequent second reason to change.

q: This class computes a sales total, formats it as HTML and writes it to a file. Which refactor applies SRP best?
options: Make all three methods static so the class holds no state
Keep total() in Report; move HTML to a formatter and file output to a writer
Create HtmlReport and FileReport subclasses that each override one method
Merge the three methods into one generate() method so there is a single entry point
why: Calculation rules, output format and storage change for different reasons. With a class for each, a new format such as PDF is a new formatter, and a storage change does not touch the totals code.
wrong: Static or not, the class still mixes three jobs that change for different reasons.
Subclasses still inherit all three jobs, and each mix of format and storage would need its own class.
One big method hides the three jobs instead of separating them.

q: ReportExporter.export() has an if/else for CSV and PDF. Each new format (XML, then JSON) means editing and retesting this shipped method. Which principle is this design working against?
options: Interface Segregation, because one method serves every format
Liskov Substitution, because CSV and PDF exporters behave differently
Dependency Inversion, because export() is called by high-level code
Open/Closed: new formats should arrive as new code, not edits
why: Open/Closed asks that a module be open to extension and closed to modification. Here every format is an edit to the same method. With an Exporter interface and one class per format, adding JSON is a new class and the tested code stays untouched.
wrong: ISP is about clients being forced to depend on methods they do not use; callers here use the one method they need.
No subclass replaces a base type here; there is no hierarchy yet.
Being called by high-level code is normal; DIP is about what a module depends on, and the pain here is repeated edits.

q: A tax class built with Open/Closed in mind has a rounding bug. A teammate says OCP forbids editing it, so the fix must go in a subclass that overrides the method. What is right?
options: The teammate is right: a closed class may only change through subclasses
Fix the bug in place; OCP is about adding features, not freezing bugs
Copy the class into TaxV2 with the fix and move callers over one by one
Leave the bug alone, because callers may now depend on the wrong rounding
why: Closed for modification means new behaviour should not require rewriting working code. A bug means the code is not working, so fixing it where it lives is correct. A patching subclass leaves the broken version in use by every caller of the base class.
wrong: OCP does not ban edits; it says new behaviour should come from extension. Bug fixes are normal edits.
Two near-copies double the code to maintain and keep the bug alive for callers not yet moved.
Keeping a known bug is rarely right; if callers depend on it, that is a separate, deliberate decision.

q: Password rules are plain functions in a list. A new rule is needed: the password must contain a digit. Which change fits this design best?
options: Write has_digit and add it to RULES; is_valid stays unchanged
Add an if for digits inside is_valid, before the all() call
Extend has_upper to also look for a digit, since it already loops over characters
Copy is_valid into is_valid_v2 with the digit check, so old callers are untouched
why: is_valid only knows that a rule is a function returning True or False. New rules plug in as new functions, so the checker does not change. This is Open/Closed in practice: extension through a list of small, swappable rules.
wrong: It works, but it edits the generic checker for every rule and ignores the extension point the design already has.
has_upper would then do two jobs and its name would lie; one rule per function keeps each rule testable.
Two checkers drift apart over time; the list already allows new rules without touching old code.

q: Bird has fly(). Penguin extends Bird, and its fly() throws an exception. A loop that calls fly() on every Bird in a list crashes. Which fix addresses the root cause?
options: In the loop, check whether each bird is a Penguin before calling fly()
Make Penguin.fly() do nothing, so no exception is thrown
Move fly() out of Bird into a Flyer type that only flying birds have
Catch the exception around every fly() call in the codebase
why: Bird promises that every bird can fly, and Penguin cannot keep that promise, so it is not substitutable (Liskov). With fly() in its own type the promise is true: code that needs flying asks for a Flyer, and a Penguin is never passed in.
wrong: A type check patches one loop; every other caller must remember it, and each new flightless bird adds more checks.
A silent no-op still breaks the promise: code that expects the bird to be in the air gets a wrong result with no error.
Catching everywhere spreads the problem; the base type still claims something its subtypes cannot do.

q: Code written for Account counts on one rule: a withdrawal succeeds when the balance is enough. It gets a LimitedAccount with balance 500 and withdraws 150. Which statement is correct?
options: No problem: a subclass may be used anywhere its base class is expected
This breaks LSP: the subclass refuses a call the base type promises to accept
This breaks LSP only because the subclass calls super().withdraw()
LSP holds as long as every caller checks isinstance(acc, LimitedAccount) first
why: LSP is about behaviour, not just types. LimitedAccount adds a stricter precondition (at most 100), so a caller that follows Account's rules gets a ValueError. Fixes: put the limit into the base contract, or do not make LimitedAccount a subclass.
wrong: That is plain subtyping: the code runs, but the subclass behaves in a way the caller was not promised.
Calling the base method is fine and common; the problem is the extra rule before it.
Type checks in callers are a symptom of an LSP break, not a fix; every new caller must remember them.

q: Interface Machine has print(), scan() and fax(). A SimplePrinter must implement it, so its scan() and fax() just throw errors. Which change fixes the design?
options: Make Machine an abstract class whose scan() and fax() do nothing by default
Keep Machine, and document that SimplePrinter does not support scan or fax
Rename the methods to doPrint, doScan and doFax so each one is optional
Split into Printer, Scanner and Fax; each device implements what it can do
why: Interface Segregation says clients should not depend on methods they do not use. Small interfaces let a SimplePrinter be only a Printer, while an office machine implements all three. Code that only prints asks for a Printer.
wrong: Default no-ops hide the problem: callers can still call scan() on a printer and silently get nothing.
Documentation does not stop the call; the type still claims the printer can scan.
Renaming does not make a method optional; the interface still requires all three.

q: A report job uses only two read methods of UserRepository, which has 12 methods including delete and update. The job's test fake must stub all 12. What is the best fix?
options: Give the job a narrow UserReader interface that UserRepository implements
Split UserRepository into separate classes, one per method, to follow SRP
Pass the job the whole database connection, so it needs no repository at all
Let the fake extend the real UserRepository and override the two methods
why: This is Interface Segregation: the job should depend only on what it uses. One class can implement both the full repository and a narrow reading interface. The job asks for a UserReader, its fake has two methods, and it cannot call delete by mistake.
wrong: ISP is about the client's view, not the class's size; the implementation can stay one class.
That couples the job to even more, the raw database, and makes testing harder.
The fake then drags in the real class and its setup, and any method not overridden still hits the real store.

q: Unit tests for OrderService need a running MySQL server. Which change applies the Dependency Inversion Principle?
options: Make MySqlOrderRepository a Singleton so tests share one connection
Move the new MySqlOrderRepository() call into a static helper method
Depend on an OrderRepository interface passed into the constructor
Make OrderService extend MySqlOrderRepository so it owns the queries
why: OrderService holds the business rule, so it should depend on an abstraction, not on a MySQL class. With the interface passed in, production gives it the MySQL version and a test gives it an in-memory fake, with no database.
wrong: It is still a hard-wired concrete class, now also global; tests still need MySQL.
Moving the new call around does not remove the dependency on the concrete class.
Inheritance ties the business logic even tighter to MySQL, and an order service is not a repository.

q: OrderService now gets its repository from the constructor, but the parameter type is MySqlOrderRepository. A teammate says: we inject it, so we follow DIP. Is that right?
options: Yes: dependency injection and the Dependency Inversion Principle are the same
Yes: any constructor parameter counts as an abstraction
No: DIP also forbids constructors from taking any parameters
No: it is injected, but the service still depends on a concrete class
why: Injection is a technique; inversion is about which way the dependency points. The high-level service still names a MySQL class, so a test or a new store must be that class or a subclass. Changing the parameter to an OrderRepository interface completes DIP.
wrong: DI is one common way to reach DIP, but you can inject concrete classes and miss the point.
A parameter whose type is a concrete class still ties the caller to that class.
Constructor parameters are how DIP is usually applied; the problem is the parameter's type.

q: Checkout code calls order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCountry().getTaxRate(). What is the main risk of this line?
options: It is slow, because every getter call allocates a new object on the heap
It ties Checkout to the inner structure of three other classes
It breaks the encapsulation of Checkout's own private fields
Nothing: chaining getters is how objects are meant to be used
why: Checkout now knows that orders hold customers, customers hold addresses and addresses hold countries. If any link changes, Checkout breaks. Asking the order for what is needed, like order.taxRate(), keeps that knowledge in one place (low coupling).
wrong: Getters usually return existing objects; the cost is coupling, not speed.
Checkout's own fields are not touched; it is the other classes whose structure leaks out.
Long chains are a known smell (Law of Demeter): each step is one more class you depend on.

q: Usernames and product codes shared one rule (3 to 20 letters or digits), so one validate_code() checks both. Different teams own them, and the rules are expected to keep diverging. Now codes must allow dashes. Best move?
options: Add an allow_dash flag to validate_code() and pass True only for product codes
Allow dashes in validate_code(), since both callers share one function
Split it back into two validators; the rules only looked alike by chance
Keep one function, but move it to a base class both validators extend
why: DRY is about one piece of knowledge, not similar-looking code. The two rules have different owners and reasons to change, so sharing one function coupled them. Separate validators let each rule evolve; a flag keeps the coupling and grows with every new difference.
wrong: A boolean flag makes one function do two jobs; each new difference adds another flag and another branch.
That quietly changes the username rule too, a bug caused by false sharing.
Moving the code changes where it lives, not the fact that two different rules are tied together.

q: A UI calls has_unread() to decide whether to show a badge. What does this print, and what does it reveal?
options: True False: the check itself marks messages as read
True True: asking a question never changes the object
False False: unread is computed after the flags are set
True, then an error: the list is changed while looping
why: The name promises a question, but the method also changes state. The first call returns True and marks everything read, so the second returns False. Keep queries free of side effects and put the change in a clearly named command like mark_all_read().
wrong: That is what the name suggests, but the loop sets read to True on each unread message.
The unread list is built before the loop changes anything, so the first call sees one unread message.
The loop changes the dicts inside the list, not the list itself, which is safe.
